content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a method for graph contrastive learning, specifically optimized for heterophily graphs. The idea of HLCL is simple: to generate contrastive pairs, HLCL uses two branches of encoders. One encoder is the vanilla GCN which performs low-pass filtering (smoothing); the other encoder is uses the Laplacian matrix as the propagation matrix so that each layer preserves high-pass filtering. The low-pass embeddings are contrasted with the high-pass ones with a standard contrastive loss (InfoNCE). The additional high-pass encoder helps preserve information for heterophilous graph. Experiments on both homophilous and heterophilous graphs show that HLCL achieves significant accuracy improvements compared with various baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths

+ The paper is well-written and very easy to read. 
+ The idea to use high-pass filters for high heterophily is reasonable. 
+ Experiments have been performed extensively to demonstrate the accuracy gains as well as ablations. 

## Weaknesses

- The novelty of the design is limited. There have been many existing works combining low-pass and high-pass filtering in GNN layers. Using high-pass filtering to address heterophily is also known in the literature. The designs of the constrastive learning architecture and loss function follow a standard protocol.  
- The overall design is simple. It would be better to include more analysis to deepen the understanding. 
- It is mentioned that the "high-pass-low-pass" encoder pair is used only in contrastive learning. Only the low-pass encoder is used during inference. It is not clear how such a design can handle heterophily during inference: regardless of the training process, the inference architecture only performs smoothing and is unable to preserve high-frequency components. 
- Experiments would be more convincing if larger graph are used. The currently included benchmarks are all very small. However, one of the main motivations for CL is that labels are expensive to obtain on *large* graphs. Achieving accuracy gain on small graphs do not fully justify the proposed CL method. 
- Experiments should follow a standard setup. For example, each dataset should come with a standard data split commonly accepted by the community. However, the authors "randomly select 10% nodes for training, 10% nodes for validation and 80% nodes for testing". As a result, some accuracy number of the baselines do not match those in the original papers (e.g., DGI on CiteSeer).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is very clearly written. The motivation is clear and valid; the architecture design is illustrated with sufficient details. 

For the quality, I think the design is sound. But the analysis and in-depth understanding is limited. 

The novelty of the paper is limited. Essentially, the method is to transfer a known architecture (GNN with different filtering functions) into the contrastive learning setup. 

The paper has included some details in the experimental setup. However, detailed hyperparameter settings as well as the tuning procedure are not described for HLCL and the baselines. Source code has not been provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper presents a simple constrastive learning method that shows some accuracy gains on small heterophilous datasets. The paper shows some potential from its evaluation. However, at its current stage, I think the paper is still below the bar of acceptance due to its lack of in-depth analysis, limited novelty and lack of evaluation on realistic, large graphs.

content.comment:
**Choice of data split.**
\
We note supervised methods under heterophily including SimP-GCN, BM-GCN, HOG-GCN, H_2GCN, CPGNN, GPNN, GPR_GNN, and GGCN ([1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]) use a 48/32/20 data split. However, this split is not realistic when labels are scarce. Following the CPGNN and GRACE papers, we used a 10/10/80 split. For this setting, there are no official splits on heterogeneous datasets, and CPGNN and GRACE ([9]) both used random splits. For DGI ([10]) on homophily graphs, we used the result from the GRACE paper, which similarly uses a 10/10/80 random split.

content.title: Response from reviewer
content.comment:
I thank the authors for providing such a detailed rebuttal and conducting additional experiments. The response has partially addressed my concerns, but some of my original concerns still remain. Thus, I prefer to keep my original score. 

In particular, I agree that contrasting the high-pass and low-pass filtering results is an original idea in the CL literature. However, since the general idea of combining different filters has already been explored in the supervised learning setting, the proposed model seems like a relatively straightforward transfer of techniques into the new CL setting. Thus, even though this particular design has not been explored in CL, I would still expect to see a bit more technical depth to be fully convinced. 

Regarding the more in-depth analysis: I appreciate the authors for providing detailed case study. This helps illustrate the different effects of low-pass and high-pass filters. However, there are still two issues: 1. The examples do not explain why contrasting the low-pass with high-pass is beneficial. There are many different ways to generate the “contrastive” views. It is still unclear why this specific form of contrastive views can work well. 2. The provided case studies are suitable to be seen as motivating examples. However, they still lack some mathematical rigor if we treat them as formal analysis. 

There are many discussions on oversmoothing in the literature. Many papers have revealed oversmoothing as an issue / property of the data (e.g., [a]) or the neural architecture (e.g., [b]). This means that changing the optimization process along (e.g., by providing contrastive views during training and then dropping the high-pass branch in inference) may not be sufficient to thoroughly address oversmoothing. I would suggest the authors compare against the analysis of [a,b] when explaining the mechanism of addressing oversmoothing in HLCL. 

Finally, regarding experiments on large scale datasets: I thank the authors for providing new results on Penn94. However, Penn94 is actually the smallest graph in the benchmark proposed by [11], consisting of only 41k nodes. This graph may not be sufficient to show the scalability of the proposed method. 

[a] Zeng et al., Decoupling the depth and scope of graph neural networks. In NeurIPS 2021. 
[b] Huang et al., Tackling over-smoothing for general graph convolutional networks. In TPAMI 2021.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging our efforts. Regarding your kind reply, we have several comments:  
1. **Regarding “different ways to generate contrastive views”**: existing ways of generating “contrastive views” differ in two perspectives: augmentations and contrastive modes.
- For augmentations, we have shown that existing augmentation methods **do not work well with non-homophily graphs.**
- For contrastive modes, [1] empirically shows that same-scale comparison works better in CL under homophily, which suggests a **Local-Local comparison for node classification**. We do include DGI in Table 2, which utilizes the Graph-Local view, and it **fails to perform well in heterophily graphs.** In general, it is unclear how to generate meaningful graph representations for heterophily graphs.
- We suggested generating graph views via **graph filters**. While different types of graph filters can be used, without labels it’s not clear how one can decide about the best filters to be used for every dataset.

Overall, we have shown that most existing ways of generating the ‘contrastive views' fail under heterophily, and our method **suggests the first approach that works for both homophily and heterophily graphs.**


2. **Regarding the over-smoothing issue:**
- During the pretraining, we use high-pass and low-pass filters **with a shared encoder** to generate filtered views for the nodes. By contrasting these views, we obtain a representation different from the one generated by **either high-pass or low-pass encoder alone**. Hence, although we use the low-pass filter for the output, the final representation **differs from the output from a normal GCN encoder.**
- Our method is not intended to **address the over-smoothing issue.** Under homophily, our high-pass filter diversifies the features while preserving the center of the distribution (Fig. 4). This helps alleviate the over-smoothing problem, but is not enough to address it entirely. Importantly, due to the above reason, the high-pass filter does not harm under homophily. Our method benefits from explicit augmentation on the low-pass filter to achieve good performances on homophily graphs. Combining both filters, our model achieves **superior performances across different homophily ratios.**  
3. **Regarding the theoretical proof of our methods:**
We note that there is no theoretical proof for graph CL. However, we refer to the recent result of [2] on contrastive learning on images, in which the authors show that CL has a guaranteed performance on the downstream performance from the perspective of augmentation overlap. Specifically, the paper shows that the downstream performance of CL representations evaluated linearly on labels (using CE loss) is bounded by the contrastive loss (InfoNCE) if (1) **Augmentation x+ of example x with label y does not change the data point’s identity**, i.e., p(y|x) = p(y|x+) (assumption 4.1) and (2) **any pair of data points from the same class can be transformed to each other with some augmentations from the set of transformations T** (assumption 4.5), i.e., t(x_i) = t(x_j), for some t ∈ T, where x_i and x_j are two examples of the same class.  
- If we **only use a high-pass filter** during CL, in high-homophily neighborhoods of a graph where nodes are connected to those of the same class, the node representations will be pushed away from their class, thus eliminating the intra-class overlapping and violating the second assumption.
- If we **only use a low-pass filter** during CL, in low-homophily neighborhoods of a graph where nodes are connected to those of other classes, the representations of nodes in different classes become similar and cannot be distinguished. Here, the low-pass filter changes the nodes’ identity and violates the first assumption.
- Our method includes **both high-pass and low-pass transformations** in augmentation space T, so assumption 2 can be satisfied in both low- and high- homophily neighborhoods. Besides, by contrasting the high-pass and low-pass filtered node representations, we prevent changing nodes’ identity, thus satisfying assumption 1.

4. **Regarding larger experiments:**
We provide additional experimental results on twitch-gamers, with 168,114 nodes and 6,797,557 edges. Our method not only outperforms the other CL models but also some of the supervised learning baselines, such as MixHop.  
| Datasets      | FBGCN        | GRACE       | DGI         | BGRL         |
|---------------|--------------|-------------|-------------|--------------|
| twitch-gamers | 70.67 ± 0.06 | 63.21 ±0.04 | 62.47 ±0.03 | 61.18 ± 0.04 |

[1] Zhu, Yanqiao, et al. "An empirical study of graph contrastive learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:2109.01116 (2021).
[2] Wang, Yifei, et al. "Chaos is a ladder: A new theoretical understanding of contrastive learning via augmentation overlap." arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.13457 (2022).

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
**More analysis for deeper understanding.**
\
First, we made a toy example to illustrate the effect of high-pass and low-pass filters and motivate using both filters in a contrastive way.
 In addition, we illustrate the importance of our contrastive structure over low- or high-pass encoder alone by swapping the encoders from other graph CL methods with a high-pass encoder. \
\
The results are shown as follows:\
      **-Explanation & toy example.**
We note that even under heterophily, some neighborhoods are more label-homogeneous and some are less label-homogeneous. In such settings, contrasting the low-pass filtered representations with their high-pass counterparts is crucial to get high-quality representations. On the other hand, under homophily, the high-pass filter prevents over-smoothing. We discuss this in more detail in the toy example below.
In appendix A.5, we added a toy example of a small graph with a few nodes belonging to two classes, where the features of the nodes in the two classes are generated from two Gaussian distributions with different means and std of 1. We considered three different homophily ratios and ran the node features through high-pass and low-pass filters for a few iterations. We see that: (1) for the high homophily ratio(Fig.3), the low-pass filter reduces the variance of the features and pulls different classes towards each other, while the high-pass filter increases their variance and eventually pulls the classes away from each other. Hence, contrasting the two filtered representations prevent over-smoothing. The figure illustration is shown in Fig. 4. (2) for a lower homophily ratio where a part of the graph has homogeneous labels and the other part has heterogeneous labels(Fig.5), the low-pass filter mainly reduces the variance of the features for the label-homogeneous part, while the high-pass filter unnecessarily mixes the class features. At the same time, the high-pass filter increases the variance of features for the label-heterogeneous part and pushes them away from the other class, while the low-pass filter unnecessarily mixes the class features. In this case, **contrasting the two filters is crucial** for learning good-quality representations. The figure illustration is shown in Fig.6. (3) Finally, for very low homophily ratios(Fig.7), the low-pass filter reduces the variance of the distributions and mixes the distributions of the features in the two classes, making them indistinguishable. On the other hand, the high-pass filter pushes away the distributions of the features in different classes. By contrasting the high-pass and low-pass filtered features, HLCL is able to distinguish the feature distributions under heterophily. The figure illustration is shown in Fig. 8.

      **-Contribution of high-pass filter vs contrastive loss.** To illustrate that the performance gain of our models comes from the contrastive structure of the high-pass and low-pass filter instead of the high-pass filter alone, we conducted new ablation studies by swapping the encoders from other graph CL methods with a high-pass encoder. Our results show that when using high-pass or low-pass alone, the model cannot achieve a good performance.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging our effective approach and extensive experiments.
\
\
**Novelty.** We respectfully disagree with the reviewer on our limited novelty and we clarify below:
\
\
      **-Contributions:** We proposed the **first graph contrastive learning method for heterophily settings**. While the high-pass filter has been used before (as we referred to in our related work and is also mentioned by the reviewer), we leveraged a **high-pass filter, for the first time, to generate graph augmentations**. **This idea is entirely novel and has not been explored before**. While under homophily, either the graph structure or features can provide enough information to predict the labels (see Table 2 of [7]), under heterophily it is crucial to take advantage of both the graph structure and the features. This is because leveraging the **difference between features in a neighborhood** is crucial to generate high-quality augmentations. Our proposed high-pass augmentation effectively leverages graph structure and features to make the nodes that have different features **distinct from their neighborhood**. Through extensive experiments, we showed that the ineffectiveness of existing graph augmentation methods that augment the features or graph structure cannot produce good augmentations under heterophily. We showed that this is indeed the main reason for the very poor performance of existing graph CL methods. 
\
\
      **-Comparison to supervised methods that leverage graph filters:** Under heterophily, nodes in the same neighborhood have different labels. Hence, having access to labels is extremely beneficial for node classification under heterophily. Importantly, existing methods based on graph filters leverage the labels to find the **best combinations of the low- and high-pass filters** that yields the best performance on a particular graph. In contrast in the unsupervised setting, the label information is not available and it is not clear how the low-pass and high-pass filters should be combined to achieve a good performance. In this setting, we leveraged the high-pass filter to generate **augmented graph views** that can be contrasted with their low-pass counterparts, without the need for parameter tuning on different graphs. This is very different from combining low-pass and high-pass filters to get the best classification performance for every individual graph, as is done in existing work. In Table 2, we added MixHop as our supervised learning baseline (we select MixHop over GCN since it performs better on heterophily graph than GCN and is also commonly used as a model baseline in graph heterophily papers like [7] and [8]). We also report the results below:

|        | Cora           | Citeseer       | Chameleon      | Squirrel       | Texas          |
|--------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| HLCL   | 82.34 ±2.7     | 71.35 ±1.4     | **49.78 ±1.8** | 34.11 ±1.9     | **65.26 ±7.8** |
| MixHop | **85.34 ±0.4** | **73.23 ±0.5** | 46.84 ±3.5     | **36.42 ±3.4** | 62.15 ±2.5     |

We believe our work provides an important direction for future work on contrastive learning under heterophily.
\
\
\
**Using the low-pass encoder for inference.** 
\
\
It is important to note that **the encoder that is trained with contrasting with the high-pass view does not suffer from the over-smoothing problem**, even without using the high-pass filter during the inference. This is because the parameters of the encoder are learned by contrasting the low-pass representation with high-pass representations. Hence, we do not need to rely on the high-pass filter during the inference. We conducted new ablation studies using different filters or combinations of filters in our final encoder. The result is shown in the table below. We can see that the low-pass encoder achieves the highest accuracy with a large gap on most datasets, and variation involving the high-pass encoder has worse performances across all datasets except Texas, which has a very low homophily ratio. This demonstrates the ineffectiveness of using a high-pass filter directly in the representation encoder.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**:
- The paper is well-written and clear.
- Heterophily graphs have gained more attention recently, and the problem they are trying to tackle is relatively novel.  
- The method is straightforward and the results are promising.

**Weaknesses**:
- My main question is how much of the reported performance gains in heterophily graphs are coming from the contrastive part and how much from the high-pass filter. What would happen if we just replace the encoder in the other graph CL methods in table 2, with a high-pass encoder?

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the novelty of the problem and our promising results.

**Contribution of high-pass filter vs contrastive loss.**
\
Indeed, the main contribution comes from contrasting the low- and high-pass filtered graph views. This is because even under heterophily, most graphs have both label-homogeneous and label-heterogeneous neighborhoods. In such settings, the high-pass filter alone cannot provide high-quality representations, and contrasting the low-pass and high-pass filtered representations is crucial. We note that for different graphs, different combinations of low-pass and high-pass filters are required to provide good representations. Having access to labels, the best combination can be learned. However, without access to the labels this is indeed not possible. We showed that contrasting the low- and high-pass filtered graph views can provide high-quality representations in the unsupervised scenario. We conducted new ablation studies by swapping the encoders from other graph CL methods with a high-pass encoder. Our results show that when using high-pass or low-pass alone, the model cannot achieve good performance. The only baseline variation that surpasses our models’ performance is GRACE with a high-pass encoder on Texas. However, Texas is a small dataset (183 nodes, 295 edges) with an extremely low homophily ratio (0.06), and is not common in practice.

**Calculating the Laplacian.** 
\
Please note that we do not need to calculate the Laplacian matrix. Instead, we can perform the message passing in an inductive manner, by aggregating the node’s representations with those of its neighbors, as shown in Eq. (3). This is the same approach used to train common GNNs on large graphs. As discussed in Eq. (1) and Eq. (3), for the high-pass message passing, the aggregation highlights the **differences** between every node and its neighbors' representations. Hence, our method will have the same complexity as conducting a normal GCN message passing with an additional message being passed. This makes our method scalable to large graphs.

**Notation.**
\
 We have fixed the typos. Thank you for pointing this out.

content.summary_of_the_paper: They argue that current graph contrastive learning methods are inadequate for graphs with ‘heterophily’ in which nodes have diverse signals. They argue this is partially due to the nature of GNNs over-smoothing node signals in neighborhoods. They propose a method of view generation for contrastive learning on graphs in which a typical GNN-encoded graph is contrasted with a graph in which differences between nodes are magnified. They do this by using a ‘laplacian matrix’ or the degree diagonal matrix minus the adjacency matrix in place of the typical augmented adjacency matrix when ‘aggregating’ signals in the typical GNN way. The laplacian matrix is used in one branch and the other uses the adjacency matrix as a typical GNN, they are in my opinion analogous to a sharpening kernel v.s. a blurring kernel. The results of these two branches are used for contrastive learning as a positive pair, with other samples being negative. They show results against benchmarks on datasets with homophily (similar nodes) v.s. heterophily, and have particularly impressive results with the latter, and studies on how augmentations compare with their method in graphs with heterophily, and how their method changes with augmentation schemes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: The strengths of the paper are that it is very clear and the results seem impressive. I don’t have particular actionable criticism that I can think of.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I believe it is clearly written and there should be no trouble in reproducing their experiment. I haven’t seen this particular idea before and believe it is novel enough, at least in application to graph contrastive learning.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe the paper is clear and concise. The technical contribution / deviation from related work is very simple, and it is hard to say it’s entirely novel, but is put to good use, and I believe it is novel in its application to graph contrastive learning at the least. The results are impressive.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a graph contrastive learning method called HLCL, which performs better than SOTA methods on heterophily graph datasets. HLCL uses a high-pass and a low-pass graph filter to generate two graph representations and then contrasts the two representations. The high-pass filter uses renormalized Laplacian matrix left, multiplying the product of the node embeddings matrix and weight matrix, while the low-pass filter uses a renormalized version of the adjacency matrix. Some experiments analyze the influence of different graph augmentation methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. In the experiment part, this paper discussed the effect of different graph augmentation methods very thoroughly.

2. The problem of heterophily is worth exploring, and there are not many works analyzing this problem very deeply. This paper provides a contrastive learning method for this problem, which has great potential.

Weaknesses:
1. Lack of explanation about the influence of the low homophily ratio on the low-pass filter, and about why HLCL works in high homophily ratio graphs. Since this paper claims that HLCL can obtain good performance, there should be some explicit explanation about why HLCL is supposed to do better on heterophily graphs. Explanation with only words is not convincing. Some toy examples or math descriptions of the influence of the graph’s homophily ratio and high- and low-pass filters are strongly suggested.

2. Confusing math notations. In 3.1 PRELIMINARIES  High-pass and Low-pass graph filters, several transpose donations are missed for vector ui.

3. Outdated SOTA result. SOTA results in Table 2 are not up to date. For example, Chameleon, Squirrel, and Texas datasets. For example, GGCN in Two Sides of the Same Coin: Heterophily and Oversmoothing in Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (accepted in ICDM 2022), whose code is open-sourced, outperforms HLCL on both Chameleon and Squirrel datasets, two datasets with heterophily graph. Only comparing HLCL with Contrastive learning methods cannot prove its high accuracy. 

4. The datasets used in the experiments are small and outdated. There are only two types of networks, i.e., small citation networks and small web page networks. This makes the results not sufficiently convincing.

5. Lake of novelty. In Interpreting and Unifying Graph Neural Networks with An Optimization Framework (www2021), GNN-LF (GNN with Low-pass Filtering Kernel) and GNN-HF (GNN with High-pass Filtering Kernel) are proposed, GNN-HF-closed has SOTA performance on Cora and CiteSeer. This paper uses contrastive learning with these two GNNs, so the novelty is marginal. Besides, GNN-LF contains a linear combination of normalized adjacent matrix and identity matrix, while GNN-HF contains the sum of normalized Laplacian matrix and identity matrix. The details of the high- and low-pass filters are very similar to this paper.

6. Bad algorithm expression. The pseudocode illustrated in Alg. 1 is meaningless. It is better to add some unique details of HLCL in Alg. 1. The current Alg. 1 seems to fit every graph contrastive learning algorithm.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper’s framework is very clear.

This paper lacks novelty. In Interpreting and Unifying Graph Neural Networks with An Optimization Framework (www2021), GNN-LF (GNN with Low-pass Filtering Kernel) and GNN-HF (GNN with High-pass Filtering Kernel) are proposed, GNN-HF-closed has SOTA performance on Cora and CiteSeer. This paper uses contrastive learning with these two GNNs, so the novelty is limited. Besides, GNN-LF contains a linear combination of normalized adjacent matrix and identity matrix, while GNN-HF contains the sum of normalized Laplacian matrix and identity matrix. The details of the high- and low-pass filters are very similar to this paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper is not so novel in specific GNN, it still proposed a contrastive learning frame for heterophily graphs, and also discussed the influence of different graph augmentation methods in its frame.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
**Small datasets.** \
Our datasets are not outdated. Indeed, all recent papers studying the heterophily setting, such as GGCN, SimP-GCN, BM-GCN, HOG-GCN, GPR-GNN, H_2GCN, CPGNN, GPNN ([1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9]) use the same datasets, namely Chameleon, Squirrel, and Texas, and we are not aware of other heterophily datasets that are used commonly as benchmark datasets. We conducted an additional experiment on a large heterophily graph, Penn94, that is recently proposed by [18]. The dataset is an online social network with 41,554 nodes and 1,362,229 edges. We compared our model’s performance with other graph CL methods. Our results show that our method outperformed SOTA graph CL methods by a large margin, i.e. 8%. We are running experiments on other large graphs in [18] and will report the results as we get them.
|          | Penn94         |
|----------|----------------|
| **HLCL** | **70.97 ±0.5** |
| DGI      | 62.85 ±0.3     |
| BGRL     | 56.57 ±0.8     |
| GRACE    | 62.53 ±0.1     |

**Novelty.** We respectfully disagree with the reviewer on our limited novelty and we clarify below:

      **-Contributions:** We proposed the **first graph contrastive learning method for heterophily settings**. While the high-pass filter has been used before (as we referred to in our related work and is also mentioned by the reviewer), we leveraged a **high-pass filter, for the first time, to generate graph augmentations**. **This idea is entirely novel and has not been explored before**. While under homophily, either the graph structure or features can provide enough information to predict the labels (see Table 2 of [7]), under heterophily it is crucial to take advantage of both the graph structure and the features. This is because leveraging the **difference between features in a neighborhood** is crucial to generate high-quality augmentations. Our proposed high-pass augmentation effectively leverages graph structure and features to make the nodes that have different features **distinct from their neighborhood**. Through extensive experiments, we showed that the ineffectiveness of existing graph augmentation methods that augment the features or graph structure cannot produce good augmentations under heterophily. We showed that this is indeed the main reason for the very poor performance of existing graph CL methods. 


       **-Comparison to supervised methods that leverage graph filters**: Under heterophily, nodes in the same neighborhood have different labels. Hence, having access to labels is extremely beneficial for node classification under heterophily. Importantly, existing methods based on graph filters leverage the labels to find the **best combinations of the low- and high-pass filters** that yields the best performance on a particular graph. In contrast in the unsupervised setting, the label information is not available and it is not clear how the low-pass and high-pass filters should be combined to achieve a good performance. In this setting, we leveraged the high-pass filter to generate **augmented graph views** that can be contrasted with their low-pass counterparts, without the need for parameter tuning on different graphs. This is very different from combining low-pass and high-pass filters to get the best classification performance for every individual graph, as is done in existing work.
We believe our work provides an important direction for future work on contrastive learning under heterophily.\
\
**Pseudocode.**
For our pseudocode, we used a similar pseudocode style to [10]. We updated it with more details.\
**Notation.** We have added the two missing transposes at the beginning of page 5. Thank you for pointing this out.

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and answer the questions below.

**Explanation & toy example.** \
\
We note that even under heterophily, some neighborhoods are more label-homogeneous and some are less label-homogeneous. In such settings, contrasting the low-pass filtered representations with their high-pass counterparts is crucial to get high-quality representations. On the other hand, under homophily, the high-pass filter prevents over-smoothing. We discuss this in more detail in the toy example below.
In appendix A.6, we added a toy example of a small graph with a few nodes belonging to two classes, where the features of the nodes in the two classes are generated from two Gaussian distributions with different means and std of 1. We considered three different homophily ratios and ran the node features through high-pass and low-pass filters for a few iterations. We see that: (1) for the high homophily ratio (Fig.3), the low-pass filter reduces the variance of the features and pulls different classes towards each other, while the high-pass filter increases their variance and eventually pulls the classes away from each other. Hence, contrasting the two filtered representations prevents over-smoothing. The figure illustration is shown at Fig. 4. (2) for a lower homophily ratio where a part of the graph has homogeneous labels and the other part has heterogeneous labels (Fig.5), the low-pass filter mainly reduces the variance of the features for the label-homogeneous part, while the high-pass filter unnecessarily mixes the class features. At the same time, the high-pass filter increases the variance of features for the label-heterogeneous part and pushes them away from the other class, while the low-pass filter unnecessarily mixes the class features. In this case, **contrasting the two filters is crucial** for learning good-quality representations. The figure illustration is shown in Fig.6. (3) Finally, for very low homophily ratios (Fig.7), the low-pass filter reduces the variance of the distributions and mixes the distributions of the features in the two classes, making them indistinguishable. On the other hand, the high-pass filter pushes away the distributions of the features in different classes. By contrasting the high-pass and low-pass filtered features, HLCL is able to distinguish the feature distributions under heterophily. The figure illustration is shown in Fig. 8. \
\
**Supervised SOTA baselines.** \
\
We emphasize that contrastive learning (CL) **under heterophily** is not expected to achieve or outperform SOTA. This is because, under heterophily, nodes in the same neighborhood have non-homogeneous labels. Hence, the graph structure or features alone are not enough to infer the labels. This is in contrast to homophily settings where nodes in a neighborhood have similar features and homogeneous labels, and hence the graph structure **or** features can provide enough information to infer the labels. Table 2 of [7] shows that applying an MLP only to features, or replacing features with an identity matrix (i.e., only using graph structure) performs similarly to GCN. This allows graph CL to obtain **near**-SOTA performance under homophily. Note that even under homophily, the performance of graph CL methods, such as GRACE, BGRL, GCA, GraphMAE, and SelfGNN ([10,11,12,13,14]) is compared to simple supervised methods like GCN and GAT ([15,16]) not SOTA supervised methods such as GCNII and GPR-GNN ([5, 17]). In Table 2, we added MixHop as our supervised learning baseline (we select MixHop over GCN since it performs better on heterophily graphs than GCN and is also commonly used as a model baseline in graph heterophily papers like [7] and [8]). We also report the results below:
|        | Cora           | Citeseer       | Chameleon      | Squirrel       | Texas          |
|--------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|----------------|
| HLCL   | 82.34 ±2.7     | 71.35 ±1.4     | **49.78 ±1.8** | 34.11 ±1.9     | **65.26 ±7.8** |
| MixHop | **85.34 ±0.4** | **73.23 ±0.5** | 46.84 ±3.5     | **36.42 ±3.4** | 62.15 ±2.5     |

Finally, we note that SOTA methods under heterophily including SimP-GCN, BM-GCN, HOG-GCN, GPR_GNN, H_2GCN, CPGNN, GPNN, and GGCN ([2,3,4,5,7,8,9,1]) use a different data split (i.e. 48/32/20) than ours. This split is not realistic when labels are scarce. Following CPGNN and GRACE, we used a 10/10/80 split. This is another reason for the gap between our unsupervised method and existing supervised approaches.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
In this paper, the authors proposed a contrastive learning framework for graph neural networks. The proposed method encodes the low-pass view and the high-pass view of a graph, respectively, and maximizes the agreement of the latent codes of the two views. To verify the rationality of the proposed method, the authors test the proposed method on several node-level classification tasks, including homophilic and heterophilic graphs. 

Strengths:
(1) The idea is simple and clear, and the proposed method is easy to implement.

Weaknesses:
(1) The rationality of the idea is questionable. In my opinion, the low-pass and the high-pass information of a graph are complementary, while the proposed method tries to maximize the agreement between them, which seems anti-intuitive. The motivation behind this strategy is not explained well. Additionally, the experimental results of heterophilic graphs do not support the rationality of the proposed method, which further enhances my concern.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: After the rebuttal phase, the scores of the paper are 3, 3, 8, 5. The reviewer giving 8 did not provide very informative comments to support this work, while the remaining reviewers' concerns are not fully resolved by the authors' reply. Both AC and the three reviewers still have concerns about the rationality and performance of the method.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting: Despite my efforts, there was no discussion among reviewers, and due to this the decision is based solely on my reading of the reviews and paper.
